messages.content:
You are a Spanish writing tutor. A first pass over a learner's draft has been made; you explain it to the learner.

The draft may contain passages in English where the writer could not say something in Spanish, and "a/b" slashes where they hesitated between options. Both are deliberate.

Every problem belongs to exactly one of two passes.

Pass 1 (fix now): the fix does not depend on anything the writer has not already made clear, and swaps a few words. Grammar, agreement, tense consistency, articles, prepositions, misspelt words; a single word that is wrong or carries the wrong connotation when the intended meaning is clear and the words as written cannot be taken another way (below); an "a/b" hesitation where only one reading fits; a slip in register (below) with one standard fix (a greeting or closing formula, a form of address).

Pass 2 (worked through with the writer): fixing it needs something only the writer can decide, or it is what the writer most needs to learn to say. Any passage left in the writer's own language or another language (they could not say it yet), and "a/b" alternatives whose readings differ and could all fit; a figure of speech, idiom or whole formula carried over word for word from the writer's language, which readers would take literally or not recognise ("we're going to have great meals" for a feast of new chapters, a letter's closing formula translated word by word), even when you can tell what it means: the writer should meet this community's own way of saying it (a short collocation with one standard fix, such as a calqued "make sense" or "have a good time", stays pass 1); a sentence whose point is unclear or left unstated (a missing conclusion, a gap in the reasoning); wording a reader could take another way than meant (below); wording off in register (below) where how to put it depends on what the writer wants (how direct to be, how to ask); problems of order and organisation. A pass-2 span is the smallest unit the writer's decision affects: for "a/b" alternatives, the alternatives; for an untranslated passage, the passage and any words that only make sense with it; for a point left unclear or unstated, the whole sentence, whose small errors are then solved in pass 2 too. Pass-1 problems outside a pass-2 span are still fixed in pass 1, even in the same sentence.

Leave alone whatever already reads naturally for this platform and these readers, including informal style, emoji and the writer's own voice. Do not polish what is fine.

Words are taken another way than meant when a reader, reaching them, would come away with a different
- attitude or feeling: praise heard as a complaint, impatience or sarcasm; warmth as coldness; a joke as an insult; criticism heard as much harsher or milder than meant;
- act: a wish or hope heard as a demand, a question as a claim, news as a request, or the reverse;
- claim: who did what, what happened, what the writer thinks or knows (for example, that they misunderstood the work);
- strength: far stronger or weaker than meant (mild surprise heard as shock, a small doubt as rejection, liking as indifference).
It counts even when the rest of the post lets a careful reader work the intent out afterwards: words are read before what follows them, and a reader who first feels criticised, pushed or misjudged has been misread, however briefly (a friend told "you've really changed" hears a reproach before the next sentence makes it a compliment). It does not count when the difference would not change how the reader feels about the post or how they would answer: a shade of tone, a synonym, words that readers of this community take exactly as meant.

Words are off in register when they are read as meant but do not suit who is speaking to whom here, by the writer's relationship to the readers and this community's manners: too demanding or pushy (a reader telling an author what to do or how fast to write; a student giving a professor a deadline), too blunt or curt, too familiar, or too stiff and formal for the place, or presuming what is not theirs to decide (unasked criticism, telling an author what their characters should do). It counts even when some people here write that way: what matters is how the one addressed feels on receiving it (pressured, talked down to, put off, kept at a distance). Casual style that this place expects is not off in register.

The writer's voice stays: casual spelling and capitalisation (all lowercase, capitals for emphasis, keysmashes, stretched letters, a missing apostrophe in a contraction), slang, emoji and the community's own shorthand, wherever fluent members of this community write that way too; so does a greeting or a word from another language used as flavour that readers will get. Names (characters, people, usernames, places, the community's terms) are the writer's: leave how they spell and capitalise them and which name they use, unless a reader could not tell who is meant. None of these is a problem in either pass. But wording carried over from English (a calque, a collocation, structure or set phrase a fluent writer would not produce) is not voice: it is a problem however casual the post.

Notes are for the writer, in English, one or two short sentences. Be specific: say how the original reads to a Spanish reader (a wrong connotation, a different meaning, a rule it breaks) and what the fix does. Quote Spanish words as they are. No praise, no filler.

Target language: Spanish. The writer's own language: English.
Where it will be posted: Email to a Spanish language school.
Who will read it: The school's admissions contact, Sra. Morales.
What the writer wants to do: Applying for the September course and asking about prices and housing.
Draft:
<<<
Estimada Sra. Morales:

Mi nombre es Daniel y yo soy de Manchester, en Inglaterra. Le escribo porque quiero aplicar para el curso de septiembre. Vengo por mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y estoy muy excitado de aprender para poder hablar con ellos.

¿Es posible que usted me envía información sobre los precios? También tengo algunas preguntas. Primero, prefiero una habitación con familia / un piso compartido, no sé cual es mejor para aprender. ¿Es el piso cerca de la escuela? Necesito una habitación tranquilo para estudiar. Segundo, ¿puedo traer mi bicicleta? Me gusta montar en bici y quiero explorar las montañas. Tercero, soy vegetariano (I'm not picky but I don't eat meat) y espero que la familia puede cocinar algo para mí. Mi novia viene conmigo el primer fin de semana.

¿Me puedes decir cuándo empiezan los cursos? Necesito una respuesta antes de fin de mes porque tengo que comprar el vuelo. Estoy seguro de que voy a tener un buen tiempo en su escuela. Mirando adelante a oír de usted.

Saludos,
Daniel Clarke
>>>

The first pass, shown on the draft. [#n before → after] is a change; ⟦#n …⟧ is a span left for pass 2.

Estimada Sra. Morales:

Mi nombre es Daniel y yo soy de Manchester, en Inglaterra. Le escribo porque quiero aplicar para el curso de septiembre. Vengo [#1 por → a] mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y [#2 estoy muy excitado → tengo muchas ganas] de aprender para poder hablar con ellos.

¿Es posible que [#3 usted me envía → me envíe] información sobre los precios? También tengo algunas preguntas. Primero, ⟦#1 prefiero una habitación con familia / un piso compartido⟧, no sé [#4 cual → cuál] es mejor para aprender. [#5 ¿Es → ¿Está] el piso cerca de la escuela? Necesito una habitación [#6 tranquilo → tranquila] para estudiar. Segundo, ¿puedo traer mi bicicleta? Me gusta montar en bici y quiero explorar las montañas. Tercero, soy vegetariano ⟦#2 (I'm not picky but I don't eat meat)⟧ y espero que la familia [#7 puede → pueda] cocinar algo para mí. Mi novia viene conmigo el primer fin de semana.

¿Me [#8 puedes → puede] decir cuándo empiezan los cursos? ⟦#3 Necesito una respuesta antes de fin de mes porque tengo que comprar el vuelo.⟧ Estoy seguro de que [#9 ∅ → lo]voy a [#10 tener un buen tiempo → pasar muy bien] en su escuela. ⟦#4 Mirando adelante a oír de usted.⟧

Saludos,
Daniel Clarke

For every change give, in this order:
- change: the change copied from the markup as "before → after", so the label stays attached to it
- kind: grammar | word (word choice, connotation, idiom) | mechanics (capitalisation, spelling, punctuation) | hole (an untranslated passage filled in) | hesitation (an "a/b" choice resolved)
- pass: 1, or 2 if on reflection the fix depends on the writer's intent: in particular when the original could be taken another way than meant (a different attitude, act, claim or strength, as the routing rule defines it) and the change picks one meaning
- optional: true when the original was acceptable and the change is only a preference
- try: true when the learner could likely make this fix themselves given a nudge (a rule they know: tense, agreement, article, word form), false when they need to be told (an idiom, a connotation) and always false for punctuation-only changes
- prompt: for try items, the nudge in English: what kind of problem it is and where to look, never the answer; else null
- accept: for try items, every replacement a learner might type that is equally correct here (including the one above); else null
- note
For every pass-2 span give a note, in English, saying how a reader takes it as written and why that is a problem (it becomes the problem pass 2 shows the writer): never a fix, a choice of fixes, or words that are not in the draft.

Reply with JSON only: {"hunks":[{"id":1,"change":"before → after","kind":"...","pass":1,"optional":false,"try":false,"prompt":null,"accept":null,"note":"..."}],"opens":[{"id":1,"note":"..."}]}

'Venir a + infinitive' is the right construction for coming in order to do something."},{"id":2,"change":"estoy muy excitado → tengo muchas ganas","kind":"word","pass":1,"optional":false,"try":false,"prompt":null,"accept":null,"note":"'Estar excitado' in Spanish usually means sexually aroused, so it would embarrass the reader. 'Tener ganas de' expresses eagerness to learn."},{"id":3,"change":"usted me envía → me envíe","kind":"grammar","pass":1,"optional":false,"try":true,"prompt":"After 'es posible que' Spanish uses a verb mood that expresses uncertainty, not the indicative. Check the verb form and the subject.","accept":["me envíe"],"note":"'Es posible que' requires the subjunctive. Also, 'usted' is not needed as a subject once the verb is in the subjunctive."},{"id":4,"change":"cual → cuál","kind":"mechanics","pass":1,"optional":false,"try":true,"prompt":"Look at the question word in 'no sé ___ es mejor'. Does it need a written accent?","accept":["cuál"],"note":"In an indirect question, 'cuál' takes an accent mark when it is a question word."},{"id":5,"change":"¿Es → ¿Está","kind":"grammar","pass":1,"optional":false,"try":true,"prompt":"Ser and estar are not interchangeable. Ask yourself whether you are describing a permanent characteristic or a location.","accept":["¿Está"],"note":"A location is expressed with 'estar', not 'ser', so 'Está el piso cerca...' is the correct form."},{"id":6,"change":"tranquilo → tranquila","kind":"grammar","pass":1,"optional":false,"try":true,"prompt":"Check the agreement between 'habitación' and its adjective.","accept":["tranquila"],"note":"'Habitación' is feminine, so the adjective must be feminine too."},{"id":7,"change":"puede → pueda","kind":"grammar","pass":1,"optional":false,"try":true,"prompt":"'Espero que' is followed by a verb in a particular mood. Check which one.","accept":["pueda"],"note":"'Espero que' takes the subjunctive, so 'pueda' is needed."},{"id":8,"change":"puedes → puede","kind":"grammar","pass":1,"optional":false,"try":true,"prompt":"Check the form of address. The rest of the letter uses 'usted', so this sentence should match it.","accept":["puede"],"note":"The letter uses formal 'usted' with Sra. Morales, so this question should use the third person 'puede' rather than the informal 'puedes'."},{"id":9,"change":"∅ → lo","kind":"grammar","pass":1,"optional":false,"try":false,"prompt":null,"accept":null,"note":"'Lo' has nothing in the sentence to refer back to, so it confuses the reader. The sentence needs 'de que voy a' without it."},{"id":10,"change":"tener un buen tiempo → pasar muy bien","kind":"word","pass":1,"optional":false,"try":false,"prompt":null,"accept":null,"note":"'Tener un buen tiempo' is a direct translation of 'have a good time' and is not how Spanish speakers say it. 'Pasarlo muy bien' is the standard expression."}],"opens":[{"id":1,"note":"Two alternatives are offered: a host family and a shared flat. They mean different things and both fit, so the writer has to choose which one they actually want. Mentioning the reason is also useful."},{"id":2,"note":"The sentence is still in English, so Sra. Morales cannot read the point about being vegetarian but not fussy. The writer needs to say it in Spanish, and the sentence depends on how they want to phrase that."},{"id":3,"note":"'Necesito una respuesta antes de fin de mes' reads as a demand with a firm deadline, which may sound pushy to an admissions contact. The writer should decide how direct to be about their deadline and how to ask for it."},{"id":4,"note":"'Mirando adelante a oír de usted' is a word-for-word calque of an English closing that Spanish readers would not recognise as a standard formula. It needs the phrase that Spanish letters actually use for this closing."}]}
